> WDYT of a label-based approach ? Instead of having `spec.ttl.ttlFrom` we could have a generic label like `sandbox.io/no-ttl-apply: true` which can be toggled by another controller ? The label `sandbox.io/no-ttl-apply` would actually represent the system's state.

I did consider annotation instead of spec field. My thought process was:
1. In addition to disable, would be good to have the ability to select start time [create|ready|some-timestamp]
2. Having in one-place makes it clear that there is only one setting. vs having to look at spec & annotation.
3. for multiple values, having in spec made sense.
4. the option of some-timestamp was necessary if we decided to re-enable after a disable. Instead of relying on too far an old time (create|retry) we can set it to current time.
5. Having explicit timestamp was declarative (vs enable where we need to track when it was toggled to enable in the status)

Alternatively i also considered having a expiryTime/ttlExpiryAt/Cleanup absolute time. If we have that we dont need anything else. 

> I'm just wondering how easily someone could bypass the TTL policy (as long as they have create permissions) now that the control of the "startTimer" is at the spec level.

Even if we have an annotation, they could still bypass the ttl. This is a larger concern around rbac beyond the scope of this feature.
/lgtm

I see, the key difference is that we can use a Validating Webhook to block non-admin users from setting a label (like sandbox.io/no-ttl-apply). We can't cleanly block users from setting a specific value in the spec. This means the security flaw is in scope and is solvable with the label pattern.

On Features:
I agree we need flexibility. We can do both:

Put user-safe options in spec: We can add `spec.ttlStartPolicy: [OnCreate, OnReady]` for users

Keep the admin-only override in a label: The WarmPool uses `sandbox.io/no-ttl-apply` (protected by the webhook) to disable TTL. AFAIK, it might be very difficult for the user to know when they actually want to start counting the timer if a Sandbox is in the pool i think this is a good use case for the label. 

This separates user intent (spec) from system state (label) and system triggers (annotation). WDYT ? 

Also, is there any default value that we are thinking of for `ttlFrom` for example, like `"infinite"` ?
/lgtm

Thanks for sharing @flpanbin  !  There's a lot going on here, and I think one of the principles of the Sandbox CRD as a _kubernetes_ project is that it should follow the kube design patterns and be relatively unopinionated.  So right now we are using PodTemplate, because that's what Deployment and StatefulSet and Daemonset do.  We're consuming the whole thing, even though _maybe_ some fields are less relevant, because we want to enable people to build more opinionated layers on top.  (For example, lots of companies build their own BigcoDeployment on top of Deployment, with just the features they want)

To move forwards I can think of these two ways:

* Have your CRD create a Sandbox type, instead of creating a Pod/Deployment/whatever-it-is-currently-creating.  Because Sandbox exposes the whole PodTemplate, this _should_ be possible today, and where it isn't we want to add fields to Sandbox.  Your CRD could live in your own repo or in our examples/ folder.  If it is in our examples/ folder it would be nice to have a README describing the key fields you don't want to expose to end-users (or other reasons for creating an abstraction on top) - there are many good reasons, it just helps to motivate _your_ CRD.
* If you think your users could use Sandbox directly, except that Sandbox is missing some fields/features, then let's figure out what those are and add them more individually.  I know status.conditions has come up before and @barney-s is adding them in active PRs, but I think we could use more use-cases for status.conditions to know what is important (for example, do you just want a Ready condition, or do you want more granular information).

Is the primary use case curation or is it "pooling" of pods to reduce launch time?

I think if it's curation we have a bunch of solutions to that, like helm / KRO / kubebuilder / kubebuilder-declarative-pattern etc.  Historically we (in kubernetes) have embraced a wide variety of solutions here, rather than picking one.

If on the other hand the use case is to pre-launch some Sandboxes, to launch them faster, then I concur that a claim might be useful.  We might also be able to support this with just Sandbox.

Good question, the general idea is to promote 3 things - Fast factory sandbox creation, separation of concerns and security for different class of personas:

1. Administrators will create templates representing different sandbox families (computer use, browser use, "Java-dev"...) including all necessary config for the users to consume in bulk when running thousands of agents. Admins have control of the image,  dependencies, config and policies in their perimeter (Also allows Admins to have more granular control managing sandbox families and life cycle)
2. Users consuming only Sandboxes from templates introduces the opportunity to limit cluster object access, also helps to simplify consuming Sandboxes by users that do not have K8s knowledge.
3. Pre-launching templates of sandbox families is definitely a way to tackle any latency

OK so maybe we should split out the Template use case and the Claim use case?  A Template could be solved with helm / KRO / kubebuilder / kubebuilder-declarative-pattern.  I can imagine that different users might want to expose different things.  I have no objection to our putting an opinionated SandboxTemplate into examples/ to experiment with, but I do think that if people want to use Sandbox but not SandboxTemplate (say because they are using helm), that is OK.

The pre-launching use case I think is very interesting, and maybe we should split that out into its own issue.  I don't know whether the right way to express that is via a Claim, or whether we make the Sandbox itself the claim (and have the controller manage a pool of Pods that are not yet associated to Sandboxes?).  WDYT?

@justinsb Thanks for the thoughtful feedback. I fully understand your viewpoint on following the Kubernetes design pattern. First, let me explain the reason why we chose custom fields instead of directly using PodTemplateSpec.
- Simplified User Experience for Development Environment Use Case: Most users only need to specify image, resources, networking, and storage. Exposing the full PodTemplateSpec pushes them into container probes, security contexts, and other advanced settings that are hard to set correctly for this use case.
- Security considerations: We intentionally limit configurable fields to avoid risky or confusing configurations (e.g., not exposing the full securityContext). This allows safer defaults while still enabling a functional environment.

I fully agree exposing PodTemplateSpec directly. The sandbox project’s scope is a general, Kubernetes-native abstraction for single-instance, stateful workloads; “developer environment” is just one use case on top of that. To improve the core Sandbox, I’d like to propose adding a few generic fields.

### Proposal: Add a few fields to Sandbox

- **networking**: Provide optional Service-level exposure and/or references to externally managed routes, without binding Sandbox to a specific ingress/gateway stack.
  - Service exposure and ports:
    - Optional `spec.networking.service` block; if omitted, the controller does not create an external Service (headless Service for discovery can remain internal).
    - `spec.networking.service.type`: ClusterIP | NodePort | LoadBalancer
    - `spec.networking.service.ports[]` with:
      - `name` (string) — aligns with container port name for mapping
      - `port` (int32) — Service port
      - `targetPort` (int32|string, optional) — defaults to the named container port if omitted
      - `protocol` (TCP|UDP, default TCP)
  - Optionally `spec.networking.routeRefs[] `to reference externally managed HTTPRoute/TCPRoute (Gateway API) or Ingress. Sandbox does not create these; it only references them and can surface reachability in status.
- **schedule**: Allow an RFC3339 shutdownTime for automatic stop. This encodes a common lifecycle action for single-instance, stateful workloads.
- **pause**: A boolean to explicitly stop the runtime (delete the Pod while preserving the object and persistent state), and resume when false. This aligns with the project’s focus on long-running, stateful, singleton workloads.
### Status implications
- If networking is added, surface reachability in status (e.g., URL/IP/ports/ready).
- If schedule/pause are added, reflect lifecycle states via conditions (e.g., Stopping, Resuming, Scheduled, Ready) so callers can reason about transitions.
### On alternative of creating a higher-level CRD example
- If it is helpful to the user experience, we can add an example controller/CRD under examples/ in the future.

We’re open to adjusting details based on community feedback.

@justinsb Let me provide more context. The original idea was to just have a `SandboxTemplate` (mostly for UX) and a `Sandbox` that references a sandbox template by name. 

However, this will cause several problems:
1. SandboxTemplate is now tightly coupled with Sandbox (Sandbox has a field that references SandboxTemplate, e.g. `spec.templateName` or `spec.fromTemplate`)
2. Users can't see the actual fields of the Sandbox without looking at the SandboxTemplate, whose content is subject to change (do we handle the upgrade case?)
3. If the controller were to copy the fields from SandboxTemplate to Sandbox spec, it violates the contract (controller shouldn't modify user's intent) 

I suggested using a `SandboxClaim` to address these problem. It allows SandboxTemplate and Sandbox to be loosely coupled, and keeps a record of the actual fields being used in the Sandbox. It also allows us to easily remove SandboxTemplate/SandboxClaim altogether if we find this unnecessary from our experiments.

@janetkuo Thanks for the feedback! You're absolutely right about smaller, focused PRs being easier to review and less risky. I completely agree with that approach. I will close the PR and submit issues and PRs separately for each feature.

## Proposal

For TTL we will support these fields:
```
spec:
  ttl:
    shutdownAt: # absolute time stamp (Takes preference over other configs)
    # relative ttl
    seconds: 100 # TTL in seconds
    startPolicy: onCreate|onReady|onEnable|never
status:
  firstReadyTime: # timestamp when ready
  expiryTime: # when sandbox would be deleted.
```

When we toggle `.spec.ttl.startPolicy` between `onEnable` and `never`, we set and reset the `.status.expiryTime`. We ignore `onEnable` setting if  `.status.expiryTime` is set. When we see `never`, we reset the `status.expiryTime`.

When `.spec.ttl.shutdownAt` is preset we ignore all other fields.

The `.spec.ttl.seconds` and `.spec.ttl.startPolicy` provides a  temporally relative ttl policies. 
Where as, `.spec.ttl.shutdownAt` provides temporally absolute ttl policy.

### Disabling TTL

Proposal is to set `.spec.ttl.startPolicy: never`
Another option is to use an annotation `agents.x-k8s.io/no-ttl-apply: true` instead since it is easier to block users from setting it using a gatekeeper policy on annotations.

But we could also have a spec.celRule, and think of this more as a policy on pod-prelaunching than an actual pool of pods.  (spec.celRule is probably not a great name, but hopefully it shows the difference!).  A policy opens up the potential e.g. for AI/statistical pod prelaunching, which would be pretty interesting IMO. 

That said for WarmPool functionality, we probably should start by standing up a benchmark that shows that pods are slow to launch - I think that would be a good milestone to get to - where we have a presubmit and/or periodic that can measure the time to launch (say) a chrome browser for selenium/playwright/some-other-web-testing-tool.

Fair point on cross-object lookups.  I do think Kyverno can do cross-object lookups - and of course custom code can do cross-object-lookups.  I think either approach would be good for the `examples` directory :-). For choosing between custom code vs Kyverno, if we did custom code I worry that we would duplicate Kyverno, which is not something I think we should take on lightly - I think we would want a high burden of proof there.  So maybe we start with Kyverno? 

That said, I would imagine that we are not creating Sandboxes in kube-system :-). I was actually wondering whether we should create a Sandbox in a dedicated namespace where security is critical?  In either case, I think we should give some clear guidance not to create privileged KSAs in the same namespace.  I think if you had to create a finite set of privileged KSAs in the same namespace a VAP would work, either by explicit enumeration in the CEL rule or with VAP parameters that block binding to those KSAs.

Reason for that is it takes unpredictable amount of time to spin up the actual underlying sandbox pods, so it is possible that the sandbox expires before it got span up. So I feel this can be a risky and confusing option to provide to users.

Agreed on starting with using spec.podTemplate in the SandboxWarmPool CRD. This also leave the door open so we can explore using spec.celRule for more advanced use case. @justinsb feel free to take a look at the below design change and concerns, and let me know.

Using spec.podTemplate in the SandboxWarmPool CRD, when a sandbox user tries to get a sandbox by creating either `Sandbox` CR or `SandboxClaim` CR (which refers to a SandboxTemplate who contains spec.podTemplate), the corresponding controller should first check whether there is an existing `SandboxWarmPool` contains the Pod which has the same pod specs as defined in `Sandbox.spec.podTemplate` or the corresponding `SandboxTemplate.spec.podTemplate` of the `SandboxClaim`. To achieve this, we need to design in a way that the SandboxWarmPool can be discovered via Pre-computed `podTemplate` Hash. This hash is calculated and injected by a webhook before the object is persisted, ensuring that identical raw templates produce identical hashes, regardless of any subsequent defaulting logic. To be detailed:

#### Mutating Admission Webhooks ####

This design requires the deployment of two MutatingAdmissionWebhooks, one for Sandbox CRs, and one for SandboxWarmPool CRs.
- Objective: To intercept CREATE and UPDATE requests for both resource types.
- Function: All webhooks will use the identical shared hashing utility (see below) to compute a hash of the raw spec.podTemplate from the incoming request.
- Action: The webhooks will patch the incoming object's metadata (label for SandboxWarmPool, annotation for Sandbox) before it is saved to etcd.

#### CRD Definitions, Labels, and Annotations Changes ####

`Sandbox`
- spec.podTemplate: <corev1.PodTemplateSpec> (Existing field for the podTemplate)
- metadata.annotations["agents.x-k8s.io/pod-template-hash"]: <hash> (calculated hash)

    This hash is added/updated by the Sandbox webhook. It serves as a lookup key for the Sandbox controller. Details see below.

`SandboxWarmPool`
- spec.podTemplate: <corev1.PodTemplateSpec> (Embedded)
- metadata.labels["agents.x-k8s.io/pod-template-hash"]: <hash> (calculated hash)

     This hash is added/updated by the SandboxWarmPool webhook. It makes the pool discoverable via a label selector. Details see below

#### Sandbox Mutating Webhook ####

- Receives a Sandbox CREATE or UPDATE request.
- Extracts the request.object.spec.podTemplate.
- Calls the shared ComputePodTemplateHash() utility to get the hash (e.g., "a1b2c3d4e5").
- Patches the incoming object's metadata.annotations to add/update agents.x-k8s.io/pod-template-hash: "a1b2c3d4e5".
- Returns the patched object to the API server.

#### SandboxWarmPool Mutating Webhook ####

- Receives a SandboxWarmPool CREATE or UPDATE request.
- Extracts the request.object.spec.podTemplate.
- Calls the identical shared ComputePodTemplateHash() utility to get the hash (e.g., "a1b2c3d4e5").
- Patches the incoming object's metadata.labels to add/update agents.x-k8s.io/pod-template-hash: "a1b2c3d4e5".
- Returns the patched object to the API server

#### Controller Logic ####
##### SandboxClaim Controller #####

**No change for the SandboxClaim controller, below are existing logic**
- The controller gets a SandboxClaim resource.
- It reads the spec.sandboxTemplate name (e.g., "my-template").
- It GETs the SandboxTemplate object named "my-template".
- It reads the SandboxTemplate spec, and use the podTemplate to create a Sandbox CR 

##### Sandbox Controller #####

- The controller gets a Sandbox resource.
- It reads the pre-computed hash from the Sandbox's annotation: `hash := sandboxTemplate.Metadata.Annotations["agents.x-k8s.io/pod-template-hash"]`.
- It creates a label selector for this hash: `selector: "agents.x-k8s.io/pod-template-hash=" + hash`.
- It LISTs SandboxWarmPools using this label selector.
- It iterates through the returned list, looking for a pool with status.availableReplicas > 0.
- If a ready pool is found: It claims a Pod from that pool and use it to back the Sandbox
- If no ready pool is found: It falls back to the "cold start" logic, creating a Pod using the podTemplate from its spec. 

   Note that the Sandbox controller will need to maintain the local cache (via informer) of all the SandboxWarmPool (within the namespace scope) and all the Pods (within the namespace scope) that have the label key `pool` present, so the controller can do list/get of SandboxWarmPool and Pod efficiently.

##### SandboxWarmPool Controller #####
SandboxWarmPool controller will add label `pool: <pool-name-hash>` to all the pod it creates.

#### Hashing Implementation Details ####
To ensure hashes are stable and consistent, the following implementation must be used by both mutating webhooks.

##### Serialization: encoding/gob ##### 
We use Go's gob encoder to serialize the corev1.PodTemplateSpec struct. This provides a stable binary representation that is not subject to the instabilities of JSON (like map key ordering).

##### Hash Function: hash/fnv (FNV-1a 64-bit) ##### 
We use the fast, non-cryptographic fnv1a-64 hash function, which is a standard in the Kubernetes ecosystem.

##### Encoding: strconv (Base36) #####
The resulting 64-bit hash (uint64) is encoded into a Base36 string ([0-9a-z]). This is extremely compact (max 13 characters) and fully compatible with Kubernetes label value restrictions.


### Concerns ###
The big concern I have with this design is around performance of fetching a Sandbox.
When user use SandboxClaim to get a sandbox, two controllers (SandboxClaim and Sandbox) are involved, and two object needs to be created (SandboxClaim and Sandbox). This increases latency because of the additional controller reconciliation loops and round trip calls to the Kubernetes API server for creating the objects.
While in the previous design where the SandboxWarmPool creates Sandbox (rather than Pod) directly, the Sandbox controller reconciliation loop and the round trip to the Kubernetes API server to create the Sandbox object is bypassed when user fetching a Sandbox via SandboxClaim, which improves the overall latency.

This is an example of a Kyverno ClusterPolicy.

This policy uses a mutation rule to automatically set `spec.automountServiceAccountToken` to false on any new Sandbox resource where the field isn't specified. This enforces the desired default at the cluster admission level.

```
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-sandbox-automount-token
  annotations:
    policies.kyverno.io/title: Default automountServiceAccountToken for Sandboxes
    policies.kyverno.io/category: Security
    policies.kyverno.io/severity: medium
    policies.kyverno.io/subject: Sandbox, Pod
    policies.kyverno.io/description: >-
      This policy ensures that if a Sandbox custom resource is created
      without specifying `spec.automountServiceAccountToken`, it defaults to `false`.
      This enhances security by preventing pods from automatically receiving
      Service Account tokens they may not need.
spec:
  # 'Enforce' will block non-compliant requests, while 'Audit' will only log them.
  # 'Audit' is recommended for initial testing.
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  background: false
  rules:
    - name: set-default-automount-token-to-false
      # This rule applies to all incoming 'create' and 'update' requests for Sandbox resources.
      match:
        any:
        - resources:
            apiGroups:
              - "sandbox.agentsandbox.dev"
            apiVersions:
              - "v1alpha1"
            kinds:
              - "Sandbox"
      # The 'mutate' block applies a strategic merge patch.
      # If `automountServiceAccountToken` is not present in the request,
      # this patch will add it and set its value to 'false'.
      # If the field is already present, its value will be unchanged.
      mutate:
        patchStrategicMerge:
          spec:
            automountServiceAccountToken: false
```


**match**: This block tells Kyverno to only apply the rule to Sandbox resources from the sandbox.agentsandbox.dev/v1alpha1 API group and version.

**mutate.patchStrategicMerge**: It applies a patch to the incoming resource. By not using any conditional anchors, it acts as a defaulting mechanism: if the `spec.automountServiceAccountToken` field doesn't exist in the incoming Sandbox manifest, Kyverno adds it and sets it to false. If a user explicitly sets it to true, their setting will be respected.

@barney-s Thanks for the mention. I'm happy to share my thoughts. 

I think we do need to manage the volume information required for the sandbox so that user data can be preserved. 

And I have a few questions and a suggestion to discuss:

#### 1. On examples vs. CRD field
I noticed there are some examples are created via KRO, where users can freely define any resources they need. Now we’re proposing to add a volumeClaimTemplates field into the Sandbox CRD, does that mean both approaches will be supported (KRO-driven vs. CRD-managed)?

How is the community thinking about the boundary between “bring your own resources via KRO” vs. “bake common resources as fields into the Sandbox CRD”? (a persistent question in my mind) @janetkuo @justinsb 

#### 2. Scope beyond PVCs

With volumeClaimTemplates added for PVC creation, do we also plan to add more fields for other resources like Configmap, NetworkPolicy or Ingress?

I’m concerned this could lead to a growing number of resource-specific fields in the CRD and make it harder to evolve.

####  3. Suggestion: a more flexible mechanism

- To avoid continuously adding resource-specific fields, could we offer a more general mechanism that lets users either:

  - Have the controller manage arbitrary namespaced resources (with lifecycle tied to the Sandbox)
  - Reference pre-created resources?

- For example, two complementary fields:

  - `additionalObjects`: users embed arbitrary K8s objects (apiVersion/kind/metadata/spec) as raw objects. The controller applies them, enforces namespace/labels/ownerReferences, and handles lifecycle.

  - `resourceRefs`: users reference existing resources by GVK/name(/namespace). The controller reads/links but does not create or delete them.

Happy to draft an API sketch for additionalObjects and resourceRefs if this direction sounds reasonable.

> > [#37](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/37) - To show how we can achieve it via compositions using KRO/helm
> Thanks for sharing the KRO composition example. I want to make sure if I understand your intent correctly.
> Are you suggesting that instead of adding networking fields directly to the Sandbox CRD, we should let users compose networking via KRO (Sandbox + Service + NetworkPolicy + Ingress as shown in PR [#37](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/37))

NW access is more varied and dependent on the production setup. We do have abstractions such as service and NW policies.
My question around a service is this, what does a service bring that a headless-service (already part of Sandbox) doesn't ? 
Re: Service options:
* Nodeport - usable only in test envs. Can test infra add it ? 
* ClusterIP - internal. Maybe headless service is sufficient.
* LoadBalancer - Since we have only one pod do we need a loadbalancer construct ? 
* Ingress - This makes the most sense since it handles multiple sandbox routing (and not load-balancing).

> Or are you proposing that both approaches should coexist:
 > * Direct approach: Users who want simple networking can use spec.networking.service
> * Composition approach: Users who need complex networking can use KRO to compose Sandbox + Service + other resources

Iam proposing we will have the second approach and keep adding in example folders. 
If we see a specific pattern repeating in examples we can propose making it part of Sandbox CRD.
I like the way @justinsb framed it in one of the comments. Would we add this to corev1 workload APIs like statefulset or deployment ? If it doesn't feel natural there it warrants deliberation when adding it here. May be it is part of a composition layer above sandbox.

> #### 1. On examples vs. CRD field
> I noticed there are some examples are created via KRO, where users can freely define any resources they need. Now we’re proposing to add a volumeClaimTemplates field into the Sandbox CRD, does that mean both approaches will be supported (KRO-driven vs. CRD-managed)?
> How is the community thinking about the boundary between “bring your own resources via KRO” vs. “bake common resources as fields into the Sandbox CRD”? (a persistent question in my mind) [@janetkuo](https://github.com/janetkuo) [@justinsb](https://github.com/justinsb)

Yes both would work. The user chooses their preferred method. They can use Helm or even their own custom templating logic to handle additional resources around a Sandbox. We are proposing making `volumeClaimTemplates` part of spec similar to statefulset because we believe some Sandbox instances would be stateful. We need the ability to preserve state for advanced use cases like `pause`.  

> #### 2. Scope beyond PVCs
> With volumeClaimTemplates added for PVC creation, do we also plan to add more fields for other resources like Configmap, NetworkPolicy or Ingress?

Great questions. Config is a tricky one that could have been done better in K8s. Lets get some real world examples of ConfigMap and Sandbox. 
Re NW policy and ingress i have shared some additional thoughts here : https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/30#issuecomment-3339509762

> I’m concerned this could lead to a growing number of resource-specific fields in the CRD and make it harder to evolve.

> #### 3. Suggestion: a more flexible mechanism
> * To avoid continuously adding resource-specific fields, could we offer a more general mechanism that lets users either:  
>   * `additionalObjects`: users embed arbitrary K8s objects (apiVersion/kind/metadata/spec) as raw objects. The controller applies them, enforces namespace/labels/ownerReferences, and handles lifecycle.

We would soon need to support templating for `additionalObjects`. This is a recurring pattern in k8s and that motivated the KRO pattern. 

>   * `resourceRefs`: users reference existing resources by GVK/name(/namespace). The controller reads/links but does not create or delete them.

What does the controller do with `resourceRefs`. Where does the logic for reading the linked resource reside ? In go-code ? 
If so we are committing to support a known set of resourceRefs. 

> Happy to draft an API sketch for additionalObjects and resourceRefs if this direction sounds reasonable.

Sounds like an interesting read.

I wonder whether this field will be used along with the one for shutdown time. @flpanbin would you also share more details about the design for state preservation? Please feel free to share a design proposal, or just send the PRs if that's easier.

@tomergee @janetkuo Thanks for the feedback and the insightful questions. I'm actively working through the design details. 

I think we should scope which data need to be preserved when the sandbox is paused at first.  it might include the following three categories:
1. External volumes (user‑managed PVCs) — MUST preserve
2. Container rootfs (writable layer) — NICE to preserve
3. Runtime state (processes/memory/OS state) — OPTIONAL

#### Phase 1: External volumes (PVCs) — simplest and maybe most valuable

Associate dependent PVCs with the sandbox resource.   

`Controller behavior:`

- On `pause: true`: delete the Pod; do not touch referenced PVCs.

- On `pause: false`: recreate the Pod with the same volume mounts.

#### Phase 2: Root filesystem preservation (container writable layer)

When a pod is deleted, the container's rootfs data is cleaned up. We need to develop a way to persist the container's writable layer data.
#### Phase 3: Runtime state (processes/memory/OS state)
Explore checkpoint/restore solutions (e.g., CRIU) to save process and memory state after the first two phases are complete.
Additionally, we might consider the preservation of GPU state in the future. 

@tomergee @janetkuo @barney-s what do you think?

Thanks for the thoughtful responses!

> What does the controller do with resourceRefs. Where does the logic for reading the linked resource reside ? In go-code ?
If so we are committing to support a known set of resourceRefs.

IMO, Perhaps two-tier can be provided: 

- Baseline (generic): allow referencing any GVK; the controller only checks existence.
- Deep (known set): for a documented allowlist, provide per-kind integration logic as needed. 

I’m inclined to defer resourceRefs for now and revisit it when we have concrete use-cases. If/when needed, we can start with a minimal “existence-only” model and evolve to other semantics later.

> We would soon need to support templating for additionalObjects. This is a recurring pattern in k8s and that motivated the KRO pattern.

Is this already `additionalObjects` in progress? If not, I’m happy to contribute.

> May be even volumeTemplate to create volume as well. Is that an anti-pattern (not being used in Statefulset) ?

Currently, we create a pod for sandbox directly. I'm little confused about  "not being used in Statefulset". It that means we will support statefulset in the future?

> * Baseline (generic): allow referencing any GVK; the controller only checks existence.

In this case:
1. What does Sandbox controller do if a resource(GVKNN) doesn't exist ?
2. Is this a dependency we wait for ? 

> * Deep (known set): for a documented allowlist, provide per-kind integration logic as needed.

In this case:
1. Are the set of resources optional or mandatory ?
2. Are they defined part of sandbox or do we refer only ?
3. are the allowlisted resources' lifecycle managed by sandbox controller ?
4. if a resource doesnt exist would sandbox fail (.status.ready == false) ?
5. If a resource exists do we read it and use some values from the resource ?

> I’m inclined to defer resourceRefs for now and revisit it when we have concrete use-cases. If/when needed, we can start with a minimal “existence-only” model and evolve to other semantics later.



> > We would soon need to support templating for additionalObjects. This is a recurring pattern in k8s and that motivated the KRO pattern.
> Is this already `additionalObjects` in progress? If not, I’m happy to contribute.

KRO has `externalRefs` that it waits for and even uses it in templating.

> > May be even volumeTemplate to create volume as well. Is that an anti-pattern (not being used in Statefulset) ?
> Currently, we create a pod for sandbox directly. I'm little confused about "not being used in Statefulset". It that means we will support statefulset in the future?

That was confusion i had. It is clear now that we cannot use PVs (volumeTemplate does not exist) in Pods/Statefulsets etc. 
We dont have a plan to layer on top of statefulset.

> 1. Are the set of resources optional or mandatory ?
> 2. Are they defined part of sandbox or do we refer only ?
> 3. are the allowlisted resources' lifecycle managed by sandbox controller ?
> 4. if a resource doesnt exist would sandbox fail (.status.ready == false) ?
> 5. If a resource exists do we read it and use some values from the resource ?

Thank you for these excellent questions, which touch on many important design points. To avoid getting bogged down in implementation details too early, We can start by assessing whether this direction is valuable.
 
I think a Sandbox may depend on other resources created or managed by users, such as  networking, storage, or configuration. These resources need exists or to be ready for the Sandbox to function correctly. The `resourceRefs` is intended to associate and declare these dependencies. It might be establish a "dependency graph" and "data source" for the Sandbox.

- **Dependency Management:** Declares which external resources the Sandbox's proper operation depends on (e.g., "requires a configmap exists or a PVC to be ready before the Sandbox can start or work normally").

- **​​Future Data Integration(imagine):​**​ We can envision future scenarios for ​​Data Integration​​, where the Sandbox declares what information it needs to read from which external resources.

The Sandbox controller does ​​NOT​​ create, update, or delete these referenced resources. It acts solely as a "consumer."

If it is valuable, I suggest opening a new issue for that deeper dive.

> KRO has externalRefs that it waits for and even uses it in templating.

Thanks for pointing out the KRO's `externalRef`. I've taken a look at KRO, this concept seems to be a great fit for the `additionalObjects` scenario I had in mind.
I see phase 1 as something we can achieve easily short-term. Please take a look at #52 related to phase 1.

Thanks for your patience @gongmax.

Few comments on the design:
* We may not need the webhook that does hash calculation.
  * I believe the intention for hash calculation in webhook was to capture the hash before defaulting happens in API server and data is persisted to etcd.
  * We may not necessarily need to do that. Both warmpool and sandbox uses podTemplate and they would be defaulted identically. So hashing the podTemplate read from the etcd store would also match. 
* When reconciling the sandbox and claiming a sandbox instance, we should make sure that 2 sandboxes dont claim the same warmpool instance.
  * To that end removing a label from warmpool instance is not a sufficient mechanism. 
  * We may need to add an explicit claimed by label to exclude contention.
Thank you @barney-s , updated the design accordingly.

This is an interesting discussion. A possible simplification could be to delegate the pod creation, rolling updates, and the pod template hash management to `Deployment`. This would simplify the `SandboxWarmPool` controller logic greatly.

The mechanism would be:

1.  Each `SandboxWarmPool` resource would manage a corresponding `Deployment` resource.
2.  The `Deployment` would be responsible for maintaining the desired number of pods, handling rolling updates when the `podTemplate` changes, and managing the `pod-template-hash` label, reusing Kubernetes' logic.
3.  When a sandbox is claimed, the `SandboxWarmPool` controller would select an available pod from the `Deployment`'s `ReplicaSet`, remove its `pod-template-hash` label to "orphan" it, and then add a `claimed-by` label to finalize the claim. The `Deployment` would automatically create a new pod to replace the one that was orphaned.

This approach would offload a lot of complex reconciliation logic to the `Deployment` controller.

Another downside of the `Deployment` approach is that, more coupled the SandboxWarmPool with the existing kubernetes primitives, the less flexibility and extensibility we can achieve in future. For example, one requirement we already get for 1P customer is to have capability to specify different service account for different pods in the warm pool. I think the `Deployment` approach will makes this harder if not impossible.

Now that we have a support for shutdownTime in #51  and pause #70 (not merged yet). 

We want schedulable [shutdown, pause, unpause].
I like some of it:
* Shutdown - we know a used case. We dont want too many sandboxes lying around forever. So we assume an upper bound on when we believe the sandbox is no longer needed
* Pause - This is like. We are setting an upper bound on when the current usage of sandbox would be completed. But we expect user/agent to resume it at some point in the future.
* Unpause - Not sure when a scheduled unpause is useful ? I can see on-demand unpause being useful (and supported via #70)

Also may be we should both shutdown and pause separately.
Shutdown in a week ?
but pause in an hour.

So the sandbox would be paused and eventually deleted (via shutdown).

You can either make it immutable, or support a simpler update mechanism.

body:
General Question on PDB requirements. Do we envision pdb for each sandbox ?
PDBs are more useful for multi-replica workloads where disruption can be tolerated. 
For sandbox, there is only one replica and not sure how we can describe a disruption budget.

Another aspect is if a sandbox doesnt have expiry time set, we could end up with a pod that is running for a long time and blocking node operations (upgrade).

Do you see a value of supporting a case where the Pod is "folded" to pre-defined minimum of resources, not deleted? Once triggered, the in-place scale-up would be initiated.

I think that leveraging in-place scale-down to fold and scale-up to unfold could simplify the settings

> For sandbox, there is only one replica and not sure how we can describe a disruption budget.

We can have a PDB spec as `maxUnavailable: 0%` so that single replica is not disrupted for a period.

> we could end up with a pod that is running for a long time and blocking node operations (upgrade).

That's the intention. The internal customer need at least 8 hours running pod without disruption. And for reference GKE honors PDBs for up to 1 hour before ignoring them during node upgrades and Cluster Autoscaler scale-downs.

> We can have a PDB spec as `maxUnavailable: 0%` so that single replica is not disrupted for a period.
> That's the intention. The internal customer need at least 8 hours running pod without disruption. And for reference GKE honors PDBs for up to 1 hour before ignoring them during node upgrades and Cluster Autoscaler scale-downs.

There is no way we can guarantee N hours of pod runtime without disruption. Using 0% is not a guarantee. We should recommend users of sandbox to handle disruption. From a sandbox controller's point of view we can mark the status as failed or disrupted if we can detect such cases.
/assign @janetkuo

Understood. PDB only prevents node upgrades and Cluster Autoscaler scale-downs. The proposal is about do the best on the offering end to save users effort, like what other open source offering such as [Agones](https://agones.dev/site/docs/advanced/controlling-disruption/) provides. But I don't have strong opinion. Leave it to user is feasible definitely.
Thanks for filing the FR. By KubeCon, we want to make it possible for users to deploy agent-sandbox to their clusters without building from source. We should push the images and cut a release.
/assign

First time setting up registry.k8s.io infra, following the instructions here: https://github.com/kubernetes/k8s.io/tree/main/registry.k8s.io

I see part of the scaffolding is already set up: 
- Adding new group: https://github.com/kubernetes/k8s.io/commit/435f9a47507d851ba8321cdee462da85b4e5da81
- Create staging registry and promoter manifest: https://github.com/kubernetes/k8s.io/commit/9eb001a2555fd45692bb922525e7830093ff182b

Just to sanity check, my understanding is that what's remaining is:
- Set up a `cloudbuild.yaml` file in agent-sandbox repo: https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/config/jobs/image-pushing/README.md#cloudbuildyaml
- Set up an image-pushing postsubmit in test-infra repo: https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/config/jobs/image-pushing/README.md#prow-config-template
- At this point, we should be publishing images to staging
- Finally, promote the staging image to registry.k8s.io following: https://github.com/kubernetes/k8s.io/tree/main/registry.k8s.io#image-promoter

Does that sound correct @ameukam?

Yes. those are all the steps needed to publish to registry.k8s.io.

But before that, what is supposed to be published ? nightly builds ? specific git tags ? (assuming SemVer system is applied)

My understanding is the following:
- The artifact will be a single image (agent-sandbox-controller): https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/images/agent-sandbox-controller/Dockerfile
- Staging builds will run on postsubmit, i.e. for every PR submission (following the recommendation [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/blob/master/config/jobs/image-pushing/README.md#prow-config-template))
- Then I assume for release/promotion we will use semver system and tag the image with the associated release version

@janetkuo WDYT?

body: @vicentefb FYI
@tomergee  FYI

@vicentefb , you are correct, this feature would use /resize subresource introduced some time ago. The in-place pod resize should GA in k8s 1.35.

We could have two stages for "pause soft":
A) Folded state = user-defined resource requests at minimum to keep runtime and handle initial request.
B) Unfolded state = "regular" resource requests user-defined in a workload (or defined by VPA).

Also wr should allow to specify:
C) Vertical Scaling Signal = what initiates the folding and unfolding. We can start from system signal, eg an iteraction initiated (request) - unfold the pod; fold it back after X min of no iteraction.
D) Desired state when applying the CR = folded or unfolded, depends on your use case.
E) Support of VerticalPodAutoscaler (VPA) = the flow should support a case in which Pod has VPA object attached of on-going rightsizing.

What do you think about it?

> [@jpawelczak](https://github.com/jpawelczak) great suggestion. Currently we use `.spec.replcias` and `/scale` subresource to implement pause and unpause. Are you recommending mapping `/scale` to set less values for cpu/mem. Or recommending `.spec.resourceProfile` ?

I would use /resize (in-place pod resize) for modifing resource requests and limts of running Pod.

Permissions: ensuring you have the right to publish under the kubernetes-sigs namespace or standard naming conventions on PyPI may require coordination with the SIG maintainers.

###  Step 1: Prepare the Package Metadata
Ensure the directory clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client contains a pyproject.toml file (standard for modern Python packaging). It should define essential metadata:

name: Must be unique on PyPI.
version: Must be incremented for every new release.
install_requires or dependencies: Lists libraries users need (e.g., kubernetes, requests).
If this file is missing, you must create it following [standard Python packaging guides](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/tutorials/packaging-projects/).

### Step 2: Install Build Tools
Install the standard tools for building and uploading packages:

```bash

pip install --upgrade build twine
```

### Step 3: Build the Package
Navigate to the package directory and run the build module. This will create a dist/ folder containing a source archive (.tar.gz) and a wheel (.whl).

```bash

cd clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client
python -m build
```

### Step 4: Upload to PyPI
Use twine to upload the newly created artifacts in the dist/ folder to PyPI.

```bash

python -m twine upload dist/*
```

You will be prompted for your PyPI API token (use `__token__` as the username and your actual token as the password).
Once successfully uploaded, users can install it via:

```bash

pip install agentic-sandbox-client
```

> Add a test in this PR or have a fast follow up. Do we have the framework set up to be able to test the python client ?

There is not currently a framework to test the python client. Also, as it stands the `sandbox_client.py` is quite specific to the `agent-sandbox/examples/python-runtime-sandbox/main.py` in that it assumes an `/execute` endpoint, assumes an exposed port, etc. That means this tests is dependent on having the python-runtime-sandbox image available to install into a sandboxtemplate and / or warmpool, and I don't believe this image has been publicly published yet.

So for an e2e test we'll either need to make this client more generic, or have a published version of the `python-runtime-sandbox` image available for the test to pull into the kind test cluster.
/kind bug

I noticed this article(https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/containers-kubernetes/agentic-ai-on-kubernetes-and-gke) about Pod Snapshots​ on GKE, which enables pod checkpoint/restore – exactly the pause/resume capability we're discussing.
Would it be possible to open-source this feature and integrate it into Sandbox?

> Do you see a value of supporting a case where the Pod is "folded" to pre-defined minimum of resources, not deleted? Once triggered, the in-place scale-up would be initiated.
> 
> I think that leveraging in-place scale-down to fold and scale-up to unfold could simplify the settings

That's an excellent point and a great approach for many scenarios where the primary goal is cost optimization.
However, the key limitation of in-place scaling is that if the Pod is restarted, the state is lost. For a true "pause" feature that can survive Pod restarts, we need a mechanism to persist the entire state of the sandbox.

@peterzhongyi is this because the controller runtime reader cache is eventual consistent? so when you reconcile pod in the sandbox controller, it could create a totally new pod other than the adopted pod for the sandbox
Hi @barney-s , thanks for your review. I updated the PR to address most of your comments, can you help to take a look again, thanks.

I recently tested the agent-sandbox and also have a similar requirement.
The default headless service created has no `ports` defined, which makes it difficult to expose the service via [istio](https://istio.io/latest/docs/ops/configuration/traffic-management/traffic-routing/#headless-services). Will be happy to see a way to customise it, or set it by default when `containerPort` is set.

For this commit: [278cb9543bb6ab99b602528ef7fcd268c8472db2](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/159/commits/278cb9543bb6ab99b602528ef7fcd268c8472db2)


## Key Changes
1. Infrastructure (GKE Autopilot)
- Resources: Added explicit CPU/Memory requests to sandbox-router (Fixes GKE Autopilot scheduling).
- Probes: Added standard K8s livenessProbe and readinessProbe for HA.
- Topology: Added topologySpreadConstraints to distribute router replicas across zones.

2. Client Logic

DNS/Internal Support: The SandboxClient now accepts an optional api_url. This enables:

- Internal Traffic: Pods can connect via K8s DNS (http://sandbox-router.default...) without public ingress.
- Local Dev: Developers can bypass the Gateway and use localhost via port-forward.

Retries: Replaced brittle connection logic with requests.Session and HTTPAdapter to handle transient 502/504 errors during pod startup.

3. Router Application

- Updated sandbox_router.py to dynamically route based on X-Sandbox-Namespace and X-Sandbox-Port headers.
- Added input validation to prevent DNS injection via headers.

4. Client API Updates

- Added `server_port` arg: Supports sandboxes running on arbitrary ports (e.g., 3000).
- Added `namespace` support: Correctly handles routing when Sandbox and Router are in different namespaces.

## Testing Verified
- Production Path: Verified on GKE Autopilot. Gateway discovery works, router pods schedule correctly.
- Dev Path: Verified local port-forward bypass using --api-url.
- Cross-Namespace: Verified Router in default successfully proxies to Sandbox in dev.

Run the client (Gateway Discovery Mode)
```
python test_client.py \
  --gateway-name external-http-gateway \
  --namespace dev \
  --server-port 8888
  ```
  
  Run the client (Direct Connect Mode) this is geared towards local dev, you'll need to first 

`kubectl port-forward svc/sandbox-router-svc 8080:8080` and then

```
python test_client.py \
  --api-url http://localhost:8080 \
  --namespace dev \
  --server-port 8888
  ```

@vicentefb Instead of port forwarding from outside, is it posible to leave the existing function _start_and_wait_for_port_forward as another tool for developer mode connection? also if you have an agent calling a sandbox from inside the cluster may be use full to have this mode in the client, WDYT?

@tomergee Mmmm yeah, you're right, keeping `_start_and_wait_for_port_forward` lowers the barrier for local dev (Minikube/Kind). But, instead of trying to port-forward to a brand-new, Pod (which gVisor was rejecting connections to), i'll port-forwarded to the Router Service.  Please see the new README for a better [idea](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/f35fc8ecb6c6d644516d8192738dbd059cfdb2c1/clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/README.md ) of the changes

`python test_client.py --template-name python-sandbox-template --namespace dev` 
Note: No `--gateway-name` flag triggers the local fallback logic). 
Meaning:  Localhost $\to$ kubectl port-forward $\to$ Router Service $\to$ Sandbox Pod

`python test_client.py --gateway-name external-http-gateway --namespace dev` 
Note: This would be "prod" mode 
Client $\to$ Google Cloud Load Balancer (Gateway) $\to$ Router Service $\to$ Sandbox Pod.

Changes here: [f35fc8ecb6c6d644516d8192738dbd059cfdb2c1](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/159/commits/f35fc8ecb6c6d644516d8192738dbd059cfdb2c1) 

Regarding the 'agent inside the cluster' use case: I've added an `api_url` parameter so they can connect directly via K8s DNS (e.g., http://sandbox.namespace.svc...). Maybe i misunderstood, but AFAIU `kubectl port-forward` is meant for external access (laptop to cluster). An agent running inside a pod should not use port-forward; it should use the standard Kubernetes DNS.
/lgtm

I'm thinking in in terms of the hierarchy/level of different constructs. In my mind, we have

0: SandboxTemplate
1: Sandbox (or Warmpool)
2: SandboxClaim

There needs to be a "merge" operation and anything defined at a higher level can override the same label/annotation at the lower layer.

(Warmpool is just a collection of Sandboxes so should be at the same level)

How are Sandbox.spec.podtemplate and Sandbox different ?

Pods should be created from a Pod Template like cookies from a cookie cutter, so pod labels/annotations should match what's specified in the Pod Template. This _must_ happen. 

Things to think about around propagating more labels/annotations to pods:

In Kubernetes convention, controllers like Deployments or StatefulSets don't propagate their own labels/annotations to their pods (propagating to history resources like ReplicaSets is fine), so this will be inconsistent with the convention. 

Additionally, when metadata is propagated from multiple sources, we need a clearly defined and documented precedence order for merging them, which adds complexity. This might cause confusion or unexpected results from users. 

We also want to avoid accidental propagation or unwanted metadata from parent resources to pods, which can have unintended side-effects, e.g., with monitoring or querying tools that select pods based on labels.

> In Kubernetes convention, controllers like Deployments or StatefulSets don't propagate their own labels/annotations to their pods (propagating to history resources like ReplicaSets is fine), so this will be inconsistent with the convention.

Since the convention is to specify the pod labels in the pod template, and currently the sandbox claim is only referring to a sandbox template, I think we can add an additional field to the sandbox claim CRD called "podLabels", which will add additional labels aside from the pod labels specified in the sandbox template. WDYT?

Also, please take a look at #162 because if it gets implemented, then sandbox claim CRD can also have a "sandboxLabels" field that add additional labels to the created sandbox.

This way, the sandbox claim's labels themselves are not propagated to anywhere.

@peterzhongyi Making pod label propagation explicit is a good direction. 

To make the purpose of the new field absolutely clear, I suggest we name it `additionalPodLabels` to make it obvious to the user that these are additional labels that will be combined with the base labels defined in the SandboxTemplate (instead of replacing).

Regarding the merge strategy, I'm leaning towards a safer approach that we _should not allow overrides_, by returning an error when there's a conflict. The trade-off is that users would not be able to use this field to change a label from the template, which is a reasonable trade-off for the added safety and predictability.

Before we implement the change, it would be helpful to understand the specific use cases for this feature. Could you or someone (@brandonroyal?) provide a concrete CUJ for this feature?

Hi @zvonkok , thanks for checking! My goal of this issue is to have something working that users can follow to install Kata on GKE cluster and then using Agent Sandbox to manage the Kata Runtime resource(s). So I'll add a link to Kata repo as a reference. Will cc you in the PR!

@shrutiyam-glitch @peterzhongyi

We could implement this by adding a `ReadyReplicas` field to SandboxWarmPoolStatus. This will help with observability and simplify client-side wait logic (e.g., in e2e tests, ref https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/164#discussion_r2566758155).

@janetkuo If we add a Snapshot Controller inside agent-sandbox, it would be responsible for List/Watch of Sandboxes and Pods, and—based on a snapshot annotation—determine whether a Sandbox needs to be processed. When required, it would invoke the snapshot provider to generate a snapshot.

After the snapshot provider’s CreatePodSnapshot API creates the Pod snapshot, it returns a snapshot ID, which is then recorded on the Sandbox object. Upon resume, the controller can mount the container rootfs using the snapshot ID stored on the Sandbox.

Add two new CRDs: SandboxSnapshot and SandboxSnapshotClass:

- **SandboxSnapshot** (Namespaced): A user-facing object that can be directly created/viewed by users, representing "a snapshot taken of a specific Sandbox."
- **SandboxSnapshotClass** (Cluster-scoped, optional but strongly recommended): Describes which backend to use (kubelet / VCI), what parameters are available, and the deletion policy.

The kubernetes python client is published in https://pypi.org/project/kubernetes/. We have an account that owns this project. You may want to set up another pypi project for agent-sandbox.

If we use `kustomize`, `extensions.controller.yaml` can be used as a kustomization patch (instead of being deployed directly), and it will look like this (only keeping the `--extensions` part):
 
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: agent-sandbox-controller
  namespace: agent-sandbox-system
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: agent-sandbox-controller
        args:
        - "--extensions"
```

And then the manifest can be applied with `kubectl apply -k`

Alternatively, we can move the controller bit to its own yaml. This requires less changes in the existing manifest structure. 

So the new installation looks like this:
```bash
# core
kubectl apply -f manifest.yaml -f controller.yaml

# extensions
kubectl apply -f manifest.yaml -f extensions.yaml -f extensions.controller.yaml
```

The characteristic of a sandbox is that it's a stateful, singleton workload that has a stable identity. This was guaranteed by the pod name (it must match sandbox name) before, but warmpool (https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/115) removes that guarantee, given that pod name doesn't have to match sandbox name anymore. We need to bring that guarantee back.

@janetkuo In #124 I have implemented the cleanup strategy in the SandboxClaim controller. I believe this design avoids the GitOps issue. 

The SandboxClaim controller (`sandboxclaim_controller.go`) takes on the responsibility of garbage collection.

- Behavior: It watches the underlying Sandbox. When it detects the SandboxExpired condition, it executes a Delete() on the SandboxClaim object.

- Cascading Deletion: Because the Sandbox is owned by the Claim (via OwnerReferences set during creation), Kubernetes Garbage Collection automatically deletes the Sandbox and all associated resources.

SandboxClaims are designed for ephemeral, dynamic user sessions (created via CLI/Portal) rather than declarative infrastructure. By cleaning these up, we prevent cluster clutter without risking stability.

@janetkuo I was thinking:
1. When adopting pods, should we only adopt ready pods? Yes, it might be slightly less latency to adopt a pending pod, but I feel only adopting ready pods is
    a. Very straightforward and easy to understand and maintain
    b. Avoid the situation when a sandbox gets a pending pod, but the pending pod eventually fails to become ready.

This gives users the comfort of knowing pods from the warm pool are always ready to use.

2. If we only only ready pods, then do we still need to use creation timestamp as tie-breaker? I think we can just adopt the first one seen by the list operation. The creation timestamp was originally used so that most of the pods are Ready instead of Pending; now if we only adopt ready pods, this becomes irrelevant.

3. What's the benefit of looking at "running" state? I believe checking the ready state is enough?

(BTW, `/cc` requests that the person be added to the list of reviewers by prow, and requires "membership".  You should just be able to mention their username and then they will probably get a notification from github, subject to their notification settings)

Since we define NW policies in template, by defn the same policy is applied to all pods.

If so why stamp out a NW policy per pod of a given template.
Could a set of policies per template cover all pods created by that template via labels ? 
@vicentefb

@barney-s that's fair, i did consider that at some point but decided to go for a nw per pod. 

1. A 1:1 mapping allows us to use Kubernetes OwnerReferences. The NetworkPolicy is owned by the SandboxClaim. When the claim is deleted, the policy is automatically garbage collected.
2. If an admin updates the SandboxTemplate (e.g., to close a port), it should likely apply only to new workloads. A shared policy would instantly propagate changes to all running Sandboxes, potentially breaking active user jobs.
3. The 1:1 model generates a unique sandbox-name-hash label for every Pod. This ensures that even if a rule is written permissively (e.g. allowing traffic from 'same-label' peers), lateral movement between Sandbox A and Sandbox B is impossible because they do not share the unique targeting label.

For example, recently I received an inquiry on: "how to setup network rules to limit egress from pods managed by the sandbox? " 

This could be achieved in many ways. You can manually create a NW that applies per template and will limit egress perfectly fine but the problem i still see is that it forces shared permissions among all sandboxes in that template, whereas in this current PR model (per claim) it's more granular. I guess if every single sandbox is identical and needs to talk to same endpoints, then per template seems fine. But if sandboxes are multi-tenant, different users, data etc. I believe this approach is better. 

wdyt ? 

Edit: now that i think about it more, would it make more sense to put this spec as part of the sandboxclaim API since i'm doing per claim nw...

> 1. @igooch it is possible to separate all the tracing code into a separate class so the core logic in sandbox client will be lighter/easier? Theres a lot of boilerplate stuff I would not put in the client, also it will be easier to maintain and test if its a separate class.

I had not considered this approach. I can test it out.

The GitOps issue comes from the `SandboxClaim` being declared in GitOps config source repo and gets synced to the cluster. (In this case, Sandbox is managed by claim but not GitOps, so Sandbox cleanup won't be an issue.) If the `SandboxClaim` controller deletes the `SandboxClaim` after shutdown time, the GitOps engine will see that the `SandboxClaim` is missing and recreate the claim, and therefore enters a hot-loop. 

We should make this behavior opt-in (e.g., `deleteOnExpiration: true`) or strictly documented as incompatible with declarative GitOps management, if we believe claim is temporal (like Jobs) and therefore not suitable to be managed by GitOps.

> > What's the benefit of looking at "running" state? I believe checking the ready state is enough?

> It's actually the opposite. Running happens before ready. A pod might be "running" (containers are started and executing) but not yet "ready" (pod is fully healthy).

So if a pod is ready, we don't need to check if it's running anymore. So maybe we don't need to check for "running" state if we only make "ready" pods adoptable?

Changes:

1. API Changes (types.go):
- Introduced `Lifecycle` struct to group expiration logic.
- Added `DeletionPolicy` enum (Retain [default] vs Delete).
- Moved `ShutdownTime` inside the `Lifecycle` struct.

2. Controller Logic (`sandboxclaim_controller.go`):
-  The SandboxClaim controller now calculates time.Until(shutdownTime) and sets RequeueAfter, removing the need to sync timestamps to the underlying Sandbox.
- The underlying `Sandbox` is now created with `ShutdownTime: nil` (runs indefinitely until the sandboxclaim controller deletes it), making it stateless. 
- Upon expiration, the controller explicitly deletes the `Sandbox` resource.
- Added logic to delete the `SandboxClaim` itself if `DeletionPolicy: Delete` is set, emitting a `ClaimExpired` event.
- Updates to shutdownTime are **no** longer propagated to the underlying Sandbox resource but the SandboxClaim controller does recalculate based on this update.

I tested the following scenarios: 

1. Immediate Expiration (Policy: Retain)

- Applied a SandboxClaim with a past `shutdownTime`.
- Result: Controller immediately deleted the underlying `Sandbox`. `SandboxClaim` remained with status False and reason `SandboxExpired`.

2. Active Sandbox

- Applied a `SandboxClaim` with a future `shutdownTime`.
- Result: `Sandbox` created with shutdownTime: nil (stateless). Confirmed automatic deletion of `Sandbox` and underlying resources occurred exactly when the timer expired. The `SandboxClaim` wasn't deleted. 

4. Auto-Deletion (Policy: Delete)

- Applied a `SandboxClaim` with past `shutdownTime` and `deletionPolicy: Delete`.
- Result: Both `Sandbox` and `SandboxClaim` were deleted. Confirmed `ClaimExpired` event was emitted successfully.

> Not seeing much discussion, why is this case needed? If there is a use case, can't user create sandbox directly?

They can, but it's mainly for the ease-of-use aspect of the Sandbox Claim CRD. It's kind of messy for a user to go back to creating sandboxes when they want to avoid warm pool. Ideally, when a user starts using Sandbox Claim, it would be nice for the user to perform most of the things on this level of CRD.

> > Not seeing much discussion, why is this case needed? If there is a use case, cann't user create sandbox directly?
> 
> This field is used in scenarios where a user wants to use a template but doesn't want to fetch a pod from the warm pool, add this field can make SandboxClaims more flexible.
> 
> @peterzhongyi , or do you have more cases about this?

The use case is for when a user wants a sandbox that is not a fresh image, but a pod snapshot that stored some previous state of the user's work. Since a snapshot is restored at the creation of the pod, we can't just give the user a pod from the warm pool anymore because those pods are all using fresh images.
